{"id": "a65a9fcc-4ca1-4e4b-b469-0db57f8fdcf2", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What is the difference between an Application Load Balancer and a Network Load Balancer?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "9f48ab65-bb86-48aa-97bf-868daff84d79", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "An Application Load Balancer (ALB) works at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS). A Network Load Balancer (NLB) works at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS). The choice mostly comes down to whether you need request-aware routing or raw speed and static IPs.

| | **ALB** | **NLB** |
|---|---|---|
| **OSI layer** | Layer 7 (application) | Layer 4 (transport) |
| **Protocols** | HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket | TCP, UDP, TCP_UDP, TLS |
| **Routing** | Content-based: host, path, headers, query strings, HTTP methods, source IP | Port and protocol only |
| **Performance** | Good, with some per-request processing overhead | Very high throughput and ultra-low latency, and it handles sudden traffic spikes well |
| **IP addresses** | Dynamic. You use the DNS name, and there are no static or Elastic IPs. | One static IP per Availability Zone, and you can assign Elastic IPs |
| **Target types** | Instances, IPs, Lambda functions | Instances, IPs, ALBs |
| **Security groups** | Supported | Supported (added in 2023), though some older NLBs have none |
| **TLS** | Terminates TLS and supports SNI with multiple certificates | Terminates or passes through TLS |
| **Client IP preservation** | Passed in the `X-Forwarded-For` header | Preserved natively, depending on target type |
| **Auth and extras** | Built-in OIDC/Cognito authentication, WAF integration, redirects, fixed responses, weighted target groups | PrivateLink (VPC endpoint services) |

**Choose an ALB when:**
- You're serving web apps, REST APIs, gRPC, or microservices.
- You need path- or host-based routing, such as `/api` going to one service and `/images` to another.
- You want WAF, built-in authentication, or Lambda targets.

**Choose an NLB when:**
- You need very high throughput or ultra-low latency.
- You need static or Elastic IPs, for example when clients have to allowlist your IPs.
- You're handling non-HTTP protocols such as TCP or UDP. Examples are gaming, IoT, and custom protocols.
- You want to expose a service through AWS PrivateLink.
- You need TLS passthrough to your backends.

A common pattern is to put an NLB in front of an ALB. This gives you static IPs and PrivateLink support along with Layer 7 routing.

I can also help you look at the load balancers in your own AWS accounts, if you'd like.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
